text.p: Less than three weeks after the new 1997 Chevrolet Corvette went on sale, General Motors Corp. said Monday it was recalling 1,400 of the muscle cars due to a rear suspension problem that could pose a safety threat.

About 500 of the vehicles have been delivered to customers, GM spokesman Kyle Johnson said Monday. GM has not received any reports of accidents or injuries from the problem, which was discovered by GM employees driving the cars.

Because of a supplier problem, the cars' rear suspension tie rod, which controls the angle of the rear wheel and tire, was not properly heat-treated, Johnson said. He declined to identify the supplier.
It will take dealers an estimated two to three hours to replace the parts, he said.
The recall mars the much-hyped introduction GM has been conducting for the new Corvette, the fifth generation of the famed Detroit sports car.
GM last redesigned the Corvette in the 1984 model year. The car was saved from extinction by a loyal group of company insiders, whose story was captured in a new book titled "All Corvettes are Red."
The new Corvette was unveiled Jan. 6 at the North American International Auto Show and officially went on sale March 7.
GM is spending an estimated $25 million on the Corvette advertising campaign, according to the trade magazine Advertising Age.

Chevrolet spokesman Daniel Hubbert said the recall was not likely to derail sales. "The car has been really well received. We've improved it significantly for 1997 and we've only raised the price $270.
The car has a base price of $38,060. The 1997 version features a new, lightweight engine, a stiffer frame, new suspension, as well as more interior and cargo room.
GM's stock edged up 62.5 cents to $57.625 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange in late afternoon.
